newsitem.title: UK: Despite Mars disaster, cooperation is space future.
newsitem.headline: Despite Mars disaster, cooperation is space future.

text.p: The failure of Russia's Mars-96 mission may have burnt up the aspirations of scientists in 20 different countries but international cooperation remains the best way of exploring space, scientists said on Monday.

Russia's launcher took $180 million worth of equipment from 20 other countries with it when it plunged back into the Earth's atmosphere over the weekend. Russia lost an additional $122 million -- none of it insured.
It was the second major catastrophe to hit space science this year, after the European Space Agency (ESA) Ariane 5 rocket was blown up after veering off course last June.

Ariane was carrying a cluster of four satellites that would have relayed information, mostly about atmospheric conditions in space, back to European universities. Germany, France and Italy bore the brunt of the $500 million losses.
Nonetheless, scientists say group efforts are the only way.
"The total cost of all these things is so enormous that you haven't got any choice in the matter," said Martin Barstow, an astronomer at Britain's Leicester University.

"I don't think that it's simply a question of cost," said Dr Jacqueline Mitton, spokeswoman for Britain's Royal Astronomical Society. "There is a genuine sense of community among the scientists working in these areas."
The U.S.-Soviet "space race" of the 1960s was more political than scientific, and scientists now realise that different countries have their own expertise to offer.
For example, the Hungarian Space Board, which lost projects on both Mars-96 and Cluster, had provided software for controlling instruments used to measure plasma in space.
British scientists have expertise in chemical analysis while the Japanese have taken interest in x-ray analysis.
The hard part is getting the equipment into space.
"What people are looking for is the launch," Mitton said.

"We are keen to collaborate with whichever space agency is sending things," said Andrew Coates of University College London's Mullard Space Science Centre, which had projects aboard both Ariane and Mars-96.
British scientists planned to announce on Tuesday what they could salvage from Ariane 5's cluster mission.
The United States is the only country that has the resources to go it alone in space -- and even so, often finds it preferable to work as part of a team.
Recent examples are the joint U.S.-Russian space station missions, although "every now and then competition takes root", Mitton said.
This week a senior Russian cosmonaut was dropped from the first U.S.-Russian crew bound for NASA's planned international space station in a power struggle over who should be in command.
The United States won in the end.
Mitton said there was another wrangle over a mission to intercept and study a comet.

"ESA have a mission which they are putting together right now called Rosetta. There was going to be American participation in that. But quite recently there was a divorce," she said. The issue -- finance.
The U.S. decided to do its own mission. "And now they are putting out a statement saying 'We will be there first' with a project called Stardust," she said.
In the end, scientists have to recognise that space exploration is inherently dangerous, no matter who is in charge.
"It is a risky business. Everyone has failures," Barstow said. "One of the benefits of having a lot of instruments on a spacecraft is you are actually sharing out the risk a bit."
